title: Malayalam Films the Rest of India Slept On
intro: Kerala has quietly been making the best films in the country. Here is where to start if you have only seen Drishyam.

films.title: Kumbalangi Nights
films.blurb: Four brothers in a half-built house in a fishing village near Kochi, and a brother-in-law who calls himself the complete man. Syam Pushkaran wrote it from years he spent in Kumbalangi, and the debut director rented a house there and lived in it for a year before the shoot. Made for ₹6.5 crore, it took ₹39 crore and got called the Malayalam film of the decade more than once. Fahadh Faasil's Shammi is the villain you have met at a wedding.

films.title: The Great Indian Kitchen
films.blurb: A new bride, a traditional house, and a kitchen that never ends: the grease, the leaking tap, the men who eat first and leave the table for the women. Almost the whole film is shot inside one house. Amazon and Netflix both turned it down over its Sabarimala scenes, so it released on a tiny Malayalam streamer and became the most talked-about Indian film of that year anyway. Hindi got its remake, Mrs., in 2025.

films.title: Manjummel Boys
films.blurb: In 2006 a group of friends from Manjummel went to Kodaikanal, and one of them fell into the Guna Caves. This is that story. About 90 percent of it was shot in a replica of the cave, checked by technicians who had worked on Kamal Haasan's Gunaa inside the real one. The first Malayalam film to cross ₹200 crore, and 10 Kerala State awards, the most any film has ever won there. You will hold your breath for the last forty minutes.

films.title: Bramayugam
films.blurb: Seventeenth-century Malabar, a folk singer stumbles into a crumbling mana, and its old lord asks him to sing. Then asks him to stay. Mammootty in black and white, playing something that may not be a man at all, won his fourth National Film Award for Best Actor. In 2026 it screened at the Academy Museum in Los Angeles, the first Mammootty film ever shown there. Do not watch it alone at night. Do watch it.

films.title: Aavesham
films.blurb: Three engineering freshers in Bengaluru get bullied, go looking for a gangster to scare the seniors, and find Ranga, a man who cannot stop talking and cannot take part in violence because he promised his mother. Fahadh Faasil running riot, in the words of one review. Jithu Madhavan wrote it in the gap while his debut Romancham sat delayed. Made for ₹30 crore, it took over ₹156 crore and became one of the biggest Malayalam films ever.

films.title: Maheshinte Prathikaaram
films.blurb: Mahesh runs a photo studio in Idukki, gets beaten up in public while trying to stop a fight, and vows to go barefoot until he has his revenge. That happened to a real man in the writer's village, who kept the vow. Dileesh Pothan's first film, shot with locals wearing their own clothes, cost ₹3.5 crore and won National Awards for Best Malayalam Film and Best Original Screenplay. Fahadh at his gentlest, and his funniest.
